finalResponse:
Begin with the sentence in the brief that does the most work: *"cut costs but not losses."* Two restructurings have already run the diagnostic; the group simply hasn't read the result aloud. Cost is the medicine prescribed when no one wants to name the disease, and the disease here is demand — a shrinking order book against a capacity that cannot shrink as fast as the revenue does. Each restructuring sized the unit for the revenue line of the year before and arrived after the revenue had moved again. That is why the cuts never catch the losses. They were never aimed at them.

And before the binary hardens — turnaround *or* exit — dissolve it. The work is eighty percent identical either way: honest numbers, separated contracts, retained people, a story a buyer or a board can believe. Run both tracks from day one, not as hedging but as discipline. Sale preparation forces the honesty the turnaround needs, and a live outside option prices the turnaround's claims better than any internal model will.

**On diagnosis: the question is not structural-or-execution, but which lines are which.** At the aggregate level the answer is always "both, entangled" — structural decline triggers talent flight, talent flight manufactures execution failure, execution failure confirms the structural story. Read three tells instead. First, are competitors growing? If the market is expanding while the unit shrinks, that's competitiveness — fixable in principle, though not quickly. If the market itself is contracting, growth is fantasy and the only plays are niche-and-harvest or exit. Second, examine backlog *quality*, not just size: part of the order book may be fixed-price contracts signed in better days — future losses already sold. Third, the accounting artifact: shared customers mean the unit may be carrying the cost of relationships whose margin is booked in sister divisions. Rebuild the P&L as if the unit were standalone before calling anything structural. Some of the loss may live in the transfer ledger rather than the market.

As for method — skip the twelve-week study. Read the order book line by line. Call the customers who left. And interview the managers who transferred out: they know where every body is buried, they're still in the building, and they no longer have a reason to be polite. They are the best consultants available to this exercise, and they are free.

**On what could sustain profit.** One test, applied contract by contract: where do customers renew without shopping the price? Where does the unit win work it didn't discount to get? In industrial services the answer usually hides in the same places — work tied to an installed base the unit knows intimately, compliance and inspection work that recurs by regulation, availability and emergency response that customers buy price-insensitively. The losses hide in familiar places too: commoditized labor sold by the hour against cheaper regional specialists, and long-dated contracts whose escalation clauses stopped keeping up years ago. Expect the honest answer to describe a unit half the current size or smaller, and say so to the board early. The credible path to profitability almost always runs through a smaller company; shrink-to-core is a partial exit wearing a turnaround's clothes, and pretending otherwise is how restructuring three becomes restructuring four.

Test the hostage claim while you're at it. The shared customers are cited as the reason the unit cannot be touched. Ask the customers whether that's true. The measured answer is usually smaller than the asserted one — and occasionally reversed: sometimes it is the profitable divisions' account strategy that the unit's losses are quietly subsidizing, in which case the group owes the unit a restated P&L before it owes it a verdict.

**On the plan.** The binding constraint is not analytical; it is belief. The organization has watched two plans fail and will meet a third announcement with well-mannered disbelief. So the first milestone is demonstrative, not operational: within sixty days, do something irreversible that no failed plan would have done — exit a sacred line, walk a flagship loss-making contract, ring-fence the unit's P&L from transfer-pricing noise, hand a named leader real authority in writing. Choose the leader the floor trusts over the one who presents well upstairs; turnarounds travel through credibility, and credibility is stubbornly local. In the same window, identify the fifteen or so people the focused unit would actually need and retain them quietly. If they cannot be held, the turnaround is hypothetical and the year should be spent on exit instead. And have the group pre-fund the restructuring envelope — severance and contract walk-aways — because turnarounds die of cash and hesitation, not of losses.

Then the year:

- **Months 1–3:** honest P&L by contract; backlog triaged into keep, reprice, or walk; the evidence standard agreed with the board *in writing* — what "credible path" must show, by when, measured how. For example: the retained core at positive run-rate contribution for two consecutive quarters by month nine, core order intake stabilized, the named team intact. The precise thresholds matter less than fixing them before anyone is attached to an outcome.
- **Months 4–6:** exits from the dead lines executed; one deep sizing to the revenue that will actually exist, not the revenue hoped for — a single cut, not the annual salami; core contribution visible monthly.
- **Months 7–9:** the proof window — core at run-rate profitability, core order intake flat or rising; discreet market testing in parallel with consolidators, strategics, and the insiders themselves.
- **Months 9–10:** the decision paper. Not month twelve. A decision taken at the deadline is taken by default, and an exit needs runway the deadline won't give it.

**On exit alternatives.** Four, in the order they usually rank. A sale to a strategic buyer or services consolidator — roll-up capital pays for density and customer relationships, and this fetches the best price if the craft is real; screen buyers for the one genuine externality, since a purchaser who competes with the group's profitable divisions walks away with customer intimacy worth more than the unit. A management buyout — treat it primarily as a diagnostic: the insiders' willingness to buy, at a price, is the cleanest signal available of whether the turnaround story is true. If they won't, believe them. If they will, ask why the group shouldn't. Carving the profitable core into a sister division and winding down the rest — frequently the highest honest NPV and the politically hardest, because it ends the unit as a story the group tells about itself. And run-off — usually the worst number on paper, occasionally the right answer when the backlog is toxic and no buyer exists; paying to stop is sometimes cheaper than paying to continue. Whichever route, put numbers rather than adjectives on separation costs and customer fallout — both are routinely overstated by those who want the unit to live and understated by those who want it gone.

**On the criteria.** Res

run.userPrompt:
A diversified group's industrial-services unit has lost money for three straight years despite two restructuring attempts that cut costs but not losses. The unit serves some customers who also buy from the group's profitable divisions, its order book is shrinking, and its best managers keep transferring out. The board has given leadership one final year to produce a credible path to profitability or exit.

Produce the turnaround-or-exit assessment and plan. Diagnose whether the losses are structural or execution-driven, identify which customer segments and service lines could sustain profit, design the turnaround plan with milestones for the one-year deadline, and define the exit alternatives and the criteria for choosing between turnaround and divestment.
